summary: This memo proposes a standard for message encapsulation, meaning forwarding one or more messages inside another. It also defines "bursting," which unpacks forwarded messages so they can be distributed, forwarded, or replied to.

plainLanguage.summary: Putting a letter inside a new envelope is easy, but the person you sent it to needs a way to open the outer envelope and use the letter inside.

subtitle: How to wrap one or more mail messages inside another, and how to unwrap them again.

tldr.problem: Forwarding mail messages inside a new message is common, but without an agreed way to mark where each one starts and ends, recipients cannot pull the forwarded messages back out and use them as separate messages.
tldr.mechanism: A forwarding agent puts each message between lines that start with a dash (encapsulation boundaries), and a bursting agent splits them apart again. Lines in the forwarded text that begin with a dash get a dash and a space put in front of them.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a proposed standard that gives interest group digests, forwarding and blind carbon copies one shared format. It also argues that distribution should be done by forwarding.

facts.label: Boundary
facts.value: A line starting with a dash (decimal 45)

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 934 as Unknown, and it records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself describes a proposed protocol and asks for discussion.

sections.title: Why Encapsulation Needs a Standard
sections.content:
A mail user agent (UA) can post four kinds of drafts: originate, reply, forward and distribute. This memo is about forwarding, where one or more received messages are formatted as part of the body of a new draft. A digest for an interest group can be seen as forwarding.

Forwarding is a form of encapsulation. Without a decapsulation step, which the memo calls bursting, the forwarded messages cannot be distributed, forwarded, replied to or otherwise processed as separate messages. With bursting, a subscriber can burst a digest, scan the headers and handle only the messages that matter.

The memo gives three motivations: there is no unambiguous standard for interest group digests, there is confusion about how blind carbon copies should be handled, and forwarding and distribution could use the same procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: If you glue several letters into one big envelope with no markings, nobody can tell where one letter ends. This memo adds clear dividers so each letter can be taken out and answered by itself.

sections.title: The Shape of an Encapsulating Message
sections.content:
Two agents act for the user: a forwarding agent that composes the draft before posting, and a bursting agent that takes it apart after delivery. A draft has a header portion and a text portion, separated by a blank line. The header portion should follow RFC 822 (RFC 822).

Inside the text portion, a line starting with a dash (decimal 45) is an encapsulation boundary (EB). The text has three parts: an initial text section (up to the first EB, often a digest's table of contents), the encapsulated messages, and a final text section (after the last EB, often a sign-off banner).

Each encapsulated message sits between a pre-EB and a post-EB. The post-EB of one message is the pre-EB of the next, and adjacent EBs with nothing between them count as one. Each encapsulated message has its own header and text, and the header must have at minimum a Date: and a From: field. Any addresses in it must be fully qualified.
sections.plainLanguage: The big envelope has a note on top, the letters in the middle, and a goodbye note at the bottom. Every letter is separated from the next by a line starting with a dash.

sections.title: Character Stuffing and the Parsing Rules
sections.content:
Existing forwarding agents ignore what happens when a forwarded message itself has a line starting with a dash. To fix this, the memo proposes character stuffing: when forwarding, if a line of the forwarded text starts with an EB, the forwarding agent outputs a dash followed by a space before the line. When bursting, an EB that starts with a dash and a space is not a boundary, and the rest of the line is output. This allows recursive forwarding.

The memo gives the rules as small finite-state automata. The forwarding automaton has two states and says that whenever a dash appears at the start of a line, a dash and a space are output first. The bursting automaton has five states. It outputs characters until a true EB is found, ends the current message, discards the rest of the EB line, and starts a new message after it.

For compatibility, the memo notes that many digests put a blank line around each EB. It recommends that forwarding agents wishing to stay compatible consider doing the same, and that bursting agents ignore blank lines after a pre-EB and (suggested) before a post-EB. A strictly conforming forwarding agent should not generate those blank lines.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter inside already has a line that looks like a divider, the sender puts a small mark in front of it so it is not mistaken for a real divider. The person opening the envelope removes the mark again.

sections.title: Blind Carbon Copies and Distribution
sections.content:
The memo describes three ways to handle blind carbon copies (Bcc:). One is to post a single draft without Bcc: fields, but then blind recipients may reply to everyone by accident. Another is to post two drafts, with the blind one having a prefix such as BCC- on the To: and cc: fields, which is often confusing. The method it suggests is to post a visible draft and a blind draft, where the blind draft contains the visible message as a forwarded message, with minimal RFC 822 headers and the Subject: if there was one.

The memo also discusses distribution (resending a received message so the recipient gets a processable original). It says that distribution by discussion group moderators through trusted pseudo-MTS agents is encouraged, but individual distribution is discouraged in the NBS mail standard and the X.400 draft, which recommend forwarding the message in the body of a new draft. This encapsulation standard supports that recommendation.
sections.plainLanguage: For a secret copy, the sender mails the normal letter to everyone, then mails the secret reader a new envelope with that letter tucked inside. That way the secret reader cannot accidentally reply to everyone.
